title: What counted as New Orleans style jazz
summary: Steinau and Allen discuss labels: Lewis, Oliver and Armstrong all under New Orleans jazz, and how bands today differ.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Let's see. Now, uh, when you go out and buy 78s or LPs, you mentioned in particular liking Joe H. Lewis's. Yeah. Did you consider that different from, say, King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band or Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five? Did you consider them part of the same tradition or?
Yeah, I did. I wasn't sure what you meant by different. No, as far as I was concerned.
You categorized it all as one under one name, general name.
Basically, New Orleans, a New Orleans style jazz.
Not, certainly not the same, but under the same rubric.
Yeah. You know, people, people say things like, that's contemporary New Orleans style. I mean, what, I'm not, 60s and 50s.
Some people have to put a label on everything. Yeah. And it's okay to put a label on things as long as you recognize that that's all it is.
Yeah, and sometimes things work very different.
I mean, bands do, I believe today, have a different approach from the 20s.
Yeah, there's been a lot of, you know, a lot of feedback, a lot of stuff exchanged among different groups. Some for the better, some for the worse.

There weren't that many people in New Orleans collection records, and I think it's a general route. Not that I knew of. Yeah, that we would categorize it as New Orleans jazz, not traditional, not any other name. And we meant nearly always the black guys when we talked about New Orleans jazz.
